Binary output issue
* According to the contribution guidelines, binary outputs should be avoided for clashes. That's exactly the issue with your clash, as it allows only two possible answers (either "In balance" or "Not in balance"). Please modify the output requirement to allow for more than two possible answers.

One possible option is to output the values of support and center of mass, in addition to the outcome.

Input / Cases
* Consider standardising all drawing lines to have the same width. If this is done, the instruction to "preserve spaces" can be removed.

* Consider providing height and width as input, instead of only n.

Constraints
* If height is introduced as an input, please swap the order of the constraints on the last line and the penultimate line, which can then be referenced as "Line [[h]]" and "Line [[h]] - 1", respectively (assuming [[h]] is the variable name used for height).

Cases
* Please include a case pair of intermediate height and width before the final pair, as the current gap between the final two pairs is quite large.

Thanks.

Truncating instead of rounding can give the physically wrong answer,. 

Consider this seesaw:
#_## 
. X

You're assuming that position 0 is the center of the first #. So the individual #s have their centers of mass at 0, 2, and 3, for an overall center of mass at 1.667.
The fulcrum is centered at 1, so it extends from 0.5 to 1.5. This is not balanced.
But if we truncate 1.667 down to 1, it appears perfectly centered over the fulcrum.

We could just as easily define position 0 as the left edge of the drawing, so that the masses extend from position 0 to 1, from 2 to 3, and from 3 to 4, while the fulcrum extends from 1 to 2. That puts the overall center of mass at 2.16667. It's still 0.1667 beyond the right edge of the fulcrum - changing the labeling system doesn't move the center of mass.

✅ Approved the contribution.

That is the logic. Perhaps you have implemented it incorrectly. The simplest way in this case is to simply calculate the center of mass. which, in this case, as the whole figure has the same density, is the average of the values of x.

I removed truncation and now compare the center of mass directly with the support interval, which extends half a column to each side of X, including both edges.

Your example is now correctly classified as `Not in balance`, since 1.667 is outside [0.5, 1.5]. Changing the coordinate origin shifts both the center of mass and the support interval equally, so the result remains unchanged.
Done: added support and center of mass to the output, h/w input, uniform row widths, reordered constraints, and an intermediate case pair.

i don't get it ,,, there is something wrong in my concept lol,, please explain

When calculating torque, measure each distance from the support to the center of mass of the corresponding group. Also, count every #, including those in the surface, since they all have equal mass.

In Validator 4, using column numbers starting at 0:

- The 32 stacked blocks on the left occupy columns 0 through 7, so their average position is 3.5.
- The four additional blocks are directly above X, at column 12.
- The surface contains 40 blocks, in columns 0 through 39, so its average position is 19.5.

The overall center of mass is therefore:

(32 × 3.5 + 4 × 12 + 40 × 19.5) / 76 = 940 / 76 ≈ 12.37.

X is centered at column 12 and represents a support one column wide, covering [11.5, 12.5]. Since 12.37 lies inside that interval, the seesaw is in balance.

Equal left and right torques about column 12 would require the center of mass to be exactly at 12. Here, the support covers an interval, so exact equality at its center is not required.
